sections.h: Why AI plans stall inside New York firms
p: Most New York companies already pay for some AI. It might be Copilot seats at a Midtown law firm, a chatbot contract at a media group, a ChatGPT Enterprise trial in a fund's research team, or a clever pilot someone built over a weekend. Access to tools is not the problem. The problem is that nobody owns three questions: where AI earns its place, which data it may touch, and who signs off when it goes wrong.

Regulated buyers feel this first. A bank or insurer licensed by the New York State Department of Financial Services cannot let client data drift into a public model, and an HR team in Hudson Yards cannot switch on an AI screening tool without thinking about Local Law 144. So projects pause at legal review and the budget gets spent on licenses nobody opens.

The AI consulting New York leaders tell us they want is narrower and more useful: a short list of uses that save hours or win revenue, a plan for the data behind them, and a pilot their own people can test.

sections.h: New York rules that shape an AI roadmap
p: Three sets of rules come up in almost every New York engagement, and we design around them from the first week rather than discovering them at sign-off.

The SHIELD Act requires any business that holds private information about New York residents to keep reasonable administrative, technical and physical safeguards. Sending that information to an AI vendor is part of the duty, so the roadmap names what each tool may see.

NYDFS Part 500 applies to banks, insurers and other firms licensed by the Department. Its final requirements took effect in November 2025, including multi-factor authentication for anyone accessing information systems and a complete asset inventory. An AI tool is one more system on that inventory, and its supplier is a third-party service provider you must assess. The Department has also published guidance on AI-related cybersecurity risk.

Local Law 144 covers employers and agencies that use automated employment decision tools for jobs in the city. It requires an independent bias audit within the past year, a public summary of results and notice to candidates.
We are not your lawyers. We write the plan so your counsel and compliance team can review it quickly and say yes or no with the facts in front of them.

sections.h: How it works: Talk, Plan, Build, Grow
p: Talk: a short fit check, then interviews with the people who do the work, not only the people who approve it. Plan: we score every idea on value and effort, check it against your data and your rules, and agree a short list and dates in writing. Build: we ship pilots on the top uses and measure them against the number we agreed. Grow: we train the team, hand over documentation, and either step back or keep building the next items on the roadmap.

sections.h: Proof: what more than 30 AI builds taught us
p: We have delivered more than 30 AI builds: custom tools, systems and automations for businesses that used to run the old way. The pilots that survive share one trait. Each was tied to a figure someone already reported on, such as hours spent on intake or days to close a month, so the result was obvious without a slide deck. We bring that habit to every roadmap we write.

faqs.q: What do we need to prepare before the first call?
faqs.a: Not much. A short list of the processes or questions you want AI to help with, the main systems your teams use and any rules you already work under, such as NYDFS Part 500. If you have an AI policy or a vendor shortlist, send it over. We use the call to check fit and suggest where discovery should start.

faqs.q: How do you handle NYDFS Part 500 when recommending AI tools?
faqs.a: We treat every AI tool as a new information system and every AI vendor as a third-party service provider. That means checking access controls, multi-factor authentication, data retention and where data is processed, then recording the tool in your asset inventory. Your CISO and compliance team get a short written assessment they can file or challenge before anything goes live.

faqs.q: Can you help with NYC Local Law 144 for AI hiring tools?
faqs.a: Yes, up to the audit itself. We help you work out whether a tool counts as an automated employment decision tool, prepare the data an independent auditor will need, and draft candidate notices. The bias audit must be done by an independent auditor, so for tools we helped choose or build, that is not us.

faqs.q: Should we build our own AI tool or buy one?
faqs.a: Buy when a mature product already does the job and your data can safely sit with that vendor. Build when the task depends on your own documents, your workflow or rules no product supports. Many New York firms end up with both: an enterprise assistant for general work and one or two custom tools for the tasks that make them money.

faqs.q: What does AI consulting in New York cost with 22 Signals?
faqs.a: It depends on scope, not on a rate card. The main factors are the number of use cases, the condition of your data, your regulatory obligations, whether we build pilots, and how much training you need. After a 15-minute call we can tell you which of those apply and send a written proposal.

faqs.q: How do you report progress during the engagement?
faqs.a: Your Signal Lead sends a written update every week: what was done, what was decided and what we need from you. Most New York clients keep one weekly call, booked at a time that suits them, and use the written updates for the rest. Each pilot ends with a short report that measures it against the number agreed at the start.

faqs.q: Which industries in New York do you work with on AI?
faqs.a: Mostly established companies with 5 to 500 staff in financial services, media, fashion and beauty, healthcare, real estate, law and professional services, plus technology and SaaS firms. We also work with founders, but our process is built for companies with real data, real staff and something to lose if AI goes wrong.
